name: Growth at a Reasonable Price
oneLiner: Looking for growing businesses while refusing to pay any price for the growth.
thesis:
Growth at a Reasonable Price, usually shortened to **GARP**, sits between two older camps. Pure value investors screen for cheapness and often end up holding businesses that are shrinking. Pure growth investors buy expansion and sometimes pay a price that already assumes a decade of it. GARP investors describe wanting the growth but refusing to accept whatever multiple the market attaches to it.

The idea most associated with the approach is the **PEG ratio** — a price-to-earnings multiple divided by an earnings growth rate — popularised by Peter Lynch as a crude way of asking whether the multiple and the growth are in the same neighbourhood. Lynch also sorted companies into rough categories: slow growers, stalwarts, fast growers, cyclicals, turnarounds, and asset plays, on the argument that the same number means different things in different categories.

The arithmetic is fragile. PEG depends on a forecast growth rate, and forecast growth rates are frequently wrong; a company that grows at half the projected pace was never as reasonably priced as the number suggested. High-growth businesses also tend to re-rate downward violently when growth decelerates, so a moderate multiple offers less protection than it appears to. None of this implies the approach works or is appropriate for any reader.
entryRules: GARP investors typically look first for a demonstrated record of earnings growth in the business itself, rather than a projection supplied by someone selling the stock.

Lynch described comparing the price-to-earnings multiple against the growth rate — the **PEG** idea — and treating a multiple far above the growth rate as a reason to walk away rather than a reason to bid.

Practitioners commonly ask where the growth comes from: more customers, higher prices, new markets, or an acquisition. The distinction matters because acquired growth and organic growth have historically behaved very differently.

Lynch wrote about categorising a company first — slow grower, stalwart, fast grower, cyclical, turnaround, asset play — because he considered the same valuation number to mean different things in each.
Debt levels and cash generation are usually examined alongside growth, on the reasoning that growth funded by borrowing carries obligations that growth funded by operations does not.
exitRules: The most frequently described exit is deceleration: growth slowing to a rate that no longer justifies the multiple being paid, whether or not the price has moved yet.
GARP investors also describe selling when the multiple expands far past the growth rate, on the view that the original reason for owning it — a sensible price for the growth — has stopped being true.

Lynch wrote about a company outgrowing its category, so that the story he originally bought is no longer the story he owns, and treating that as a reason to re-examine rather than to hold automatically.
A thesis broken by the business — a lost distribution deal, a competitor arriving, margins compressing — is treated in this literature as an exit independent of price.
riskManagement: The whole approach rests on an estimated growth rate, and estimated growth rates are routinely too high. A PEG that looked reasonable at a 25 percent forecast looks very different at 10 percent actual.

Growth companies re-rate sharply when they disappoint. Drawdowns of half or more in a single reporting season are well documented in this category, and a moderate entry multiple has not historically prevented them.
A moderate PEG can be produced by a temporarily depressed multiple on a business in decline, which puts GARP investors at risk of the same **value trap** that catches value investors.
Practitioners describe diversifying across several such positions precisely because individual growth forecasts fail often, and describe avoiding leverage for the same reason.
The **riskLevel** here is a rough comparative signal against the other strategies in this app, not a measurement of anyone's actual risk and not a statement about suitability.
